candidates.title: Television Broadcasting Services Des Moines, Iowa
candidates.raw_excerpt: This document proposes to amend the Table of TV Allotments (Table) of the Federal Communications Commission's (Commission) rules in response to a petition for rulemaking filed by Iowa Public Broadcasting Board (Licensee), the licensee of noncommercial educational PBS member television station KDIN-TV (KDIN-TV), Des Moines, Iowa (Des Moines). The Licensee holds a construction permit (CP) to construct a facility on UHF channel *34 at Des Moines, and now requests to substitute VHF channel *11 for UHF channel *34 in the Table, with the technical parameters as set forth in KDIN-TV's current license. The Media Bureau previously granted a petition for rulemaking submitted by the Licensee to substitute UHF channel *34 in place of VHF channel *11 at Des Moines. The Licensee states that it is now unable to complete construction of the channel *34 facility within the time specified on the construction permit, and therefore requests amendment of the Table to allow it to continue to operate on VHF channel *11 at its currently licensed technical parameters to provide uninterrupted service to viewers. Given that the Licensee proposes to utilize its currently licensed parameters, we believe VHF channel *11 can be substituted for UHF channel *34 at Des Moines as proposed, in compliance with the principal community coverage requirements. In addition, we find that this channel change meets the technical requirements as well as the Commission's interference protection requirements.

candidates.title: Returning samples from a Mars moon: Inside the science of Japan's bold MMX mission
candidates.raw_excerpt: Japan's mission to Mars is one of the most ambitious in spaceflight history. It aims to become the first spacecraft to return to Earth from Mars orbit, carrying with it the first-ever samples from the Red Planet system. The mission, known as Martian Moons eXploration (MMX), is a first-of-its-kind endeavor to study the origin of Mars' moons Phobos and Deimos. The robust undertaking includes a landing on Phobos to collect the samples — which will likely be the first from the Mars system to return to Earth — and a search for evidence that could shed light on events during the formation of the solar system billions of years ago. MMX is scheduled to launch on an H3 rocket from Japan's Tanegashima Space Center on Monday (Oct. 19) at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. local time in Japan, Oct. 20). After a 10-month journey to reach Mars, the spacecraft will spend about three years studying Phobos, deploying a rover and landing to collect its samples. The mission will then shift its focus to Deimos for a series of flybys before departing for Earth in November 2030. If all goes according to plan, the MMX sample-return capsule is scheduled to land in Australia in 2031. The spacecraft The MMX spacecraft is comprised of three main parts, as well as a small rover. After release from its H3 launch vehicle, a propulsion module will provide the boost to put MMX on course for Mars. MMX's main exploration module carries the microwave-size IDEFIX rover and most of the mission's scientific instruments, while the return module houses the sample-return capsule. Japan's Mitsubishi Electric built MMX's three main modules, with the French space agency CNES (Centre National d'Études Spatiales) and Germany's DLR (Deutsches Zentrum für Luft-und Raumfahrt) jointly developing IDEFIX . The little rover is named for a dog in the 1960s French comic "Asterix," in a nod to the country's first satellite , Astérix, which launched in 1965. candidates.raw_excerpt: On Oct. 18, 1963, a cat went to space! Félicette was a French "catstronaut" who became the first and only feline to fly to space. While the U.S. and Soviet Union were busy launching primates, dogs and humans, the French decided to join the space race by launching a cat. Félicette, a stray tuxedo cat from the streets of Paris, was a substitute for another cat named Felix, who somehow escaped on launch day. So Félicette went where no cat had ever gone before. She boarded a French Véronique AG1 rocket and soared 130 miles above the Earth before safely parachuting back down. Luckily Félicette made it home alive and well, unlike many of the other animal astronauts that flew during the space race. Félicette, the first cat to fly into space in October 1963, is seen her carrier pre-flight. (Image credit: Wikimedia Commons ) Why it mattered Félicette survived spaceflight, but was short of this world. She was euthanized two months after her recovery so scientists could study her brain. A second cat was launched by the French on Oct. 24, but its flight did not go so well, veering off course. When the cat was found a day later, it was discovered it have died as a result of the journey. From there on, CERMA (Centre d'Enseignement et de Recherches de Médecine Aéronautique) changed its research to flying monkeys. Félicette may have become a footnote to history had it not been for a crowdfunded effort to raise a statue in her memory nearly 60 years later. The sculpture was unveiled in 2019 at the International Space University in Strasbourg, France. European astronauts Helen Sharman, Paolo Nespoli and Reinhold Ewald were on hand for its reveal. candidates.raw_excerpt: Astronomers estimate that our home galaxy, the Milky Way, has churned out more than 10 million black holes over its 13-billion-year history. Yet so far, they have found only 70. Now, a group of astronomers in the U.K. is trying to close that vast gap by enlisting the public. Their project, called Black Hole Hunters , is looking for volunteers with a computer and a few spare minutes to sift through troves of data gathered by a NASA space telescope. By flagging recognizable patterns that could point to a "missing" black hole , volunteers can help fast-track a search that would otherwise take years, the team says. "You'll be narrowing down precisely where we need to point our telescopes next," project co-lead Adam McMaster, an astronomer at the University of Southampton in the U.K., said in a statement , "and you might be the one to discover a black hole." Cosmic magnifying glasses Black holes form when massive stars roughly 20 times heavier than our sun run out of fuel and collapse, leaving behind an abyss with gravity so immense that even light cannot escape. While invisible themselves, these cosmic behemoths reveal their presence by bending the light of nearby objects, and the Black Hole Hunters project is searching for one specific manifestation of this effect. It happens thanks to the fact that massive stars often form in pairs , and a star can sometimes survive the violent supernova explosion that turns its companion into a black hole. When that happens, the two bodies continue to orbit each other. If such a duo aligns just right with Earth, the black hole will periodically pass directly between its companion star and our planet. And when it does, the black hole's gravity acts like a cosmic magnifying glass , bending and magnifying the star's light, causing it to briefly appear brighter to watchful telescopes. candidates.title: Time's up for the leap second
candidates.raw_excerpt:
The world is about to stop adding leap seconds. 

Under the new system, clocks will be allowed to drift from the Earth's actual rotation by up to an hour before anyone has to step in. This means no more leap seconds – for centuries.

Leap seconds have been added to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) to keep it aligned with Earth's irregular rotation. But these adjustments can disrupt digital systems that rely on continuous, precise timekeeping. Since the practice began, 27 leap seconds have been inserted. In 2012, a leap second reportedly caused outages across more than 2,000 networks worldwide. In 2015, the US Intercontinental Exchange halted trading for more than 60 minutes.

The risk of a negative leap second – removing a second rather than adding one – has also raised concerns, as computer systems have never had to implement one on a global scale.

The reform comes after the 28th General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM), held in Versailles, France, adopted a resolution this month to introduce continuous UTC from May 20, 2027.

Sometimes described as a shift from leap seconds to a "leap hour," the change is expected to cut maintenance and testing costs for internet services, cloud computing and financial markets.

For most people, the impact will be negligible. Astronomical observations and other applications that depend on Earth's rotation can keep using data that accounts for the difference between the two time scales.

Orionid meteors are best spotted between the hours of midnight and dawn on Oct. 22, when 10-20 shooting stars may be seen brightening the night sky each hour under ideal dark-sky. The glare cast by the 74%-lit waxing gibbous moon will hide fainter shooting stars for much of the night. For the best views look 40-90 degrees away from the radiant, where the glowing trains left in the wake of the fast-moving meteors will be at their longest. Be sure to head away from artificial lights and allow 20-30 minutes for your eyes to fully adapt to the dark for the best What causes the Orionid meteor shower? The Orionid meteor shower is active each year as Earth passes through the stream of debris left behind by Comet 1P/Halley , which was observed by a fleet of spacecraft when it last visited the inner solar system in 1986. As I've grown into stargazing, I've become much more selective. The Orionids peak next week, and normally I'd be tempted. These fast meteors come from debris from Halley's Comet , which is enough of a connection to make almost anyone want to go outside. candidates.title: ESPI Calls for Stronger European Controls for MSS Spectrum
candidates.raw_excerpt: As Europe plans to reserve a portion of its mobile satellite services (MSS) spectrum authorization for European operators, a European think tank argues it should go further and maximize European control across the space segment as well. In a new policy brief released this week, the European Space Policy Institute (ESPI) argues Europe needs to take a full-stack approach to building a truly European service, meaning “at minimum” European mobile network operators (MNOs), satellite operators, and spacecraft manufacturers. The brief addresses the European Commission’s 2 GHz MSS proposal , which will determine which entities will hold the licenses to use critical MSS spectrum in Europe. Currently, Inmarsat, now part of Viasat, and Solaris, now part of EchoStar, hold the licenses. EchoStar’s spectrum was part of the SpaceX spectrum purchase. ESPI noted the reports of European MNOs making a joint bid for the spectrum, arguing this could lead to an outcome where the spectrum goes to a group partnering with a non-European satellite operator for the direct-to-device (D2D) capability. The report calls this a “quasi-sovereign outcome” and calls for the EC to keep room in the market for small and medium enterprises to participate and remove barriers to entry for new European D2D solutions. “Reserving spectrum for European operators is a welcome step, but it is not enough,” wrote Elisabeth Clemmons, ESPI research fellow. “If European spectrum and European brands end up unlocking scale for foreign space assets, Europe will have kept the label and lost the substance. That is why we need a full-stack approach.” The post ESPI Calls for Stronger European Controls for MSS Spectrum appeared first on Via Satellite .
